meta.title: FlyUp — "Pilot Profile — ADAPT" Personality Test
meta.inspiredBy: Forced-choice quad personality questionnaires (APQ / OPQ / PAPI style), as used in the ADAPT battery (Symbiotics) — not a reproduction of the proprietary instrument.
meta.disclaimer: Training tool inspired by forced-choice quad personality questionnaires (APQ / OPQ / PAPI style), as used in the ADAPT battery (Symbiotics). It has no clinical diagnostic value and is not a reproduction of an existing proprietary test.

dimensionScore.description: For each dimension, score = (number of times the statement from this dimension was picked as 'most like me') / (number of times a statement from this dimension was offered). timesOffered is mathematically constant at 40 per dimension (10 statements x 4 appearances each), computed only over the 100 non-control items (isControl == false).
dimensionScore.timesOffered: always 40 for every dimension (10 statements x 4 repeats), ids 1-100 only
dimensionScore.timesChosen: count of items where the option whose dimension == code was picked

consistencyCheck.description: For each control item (id 101-110), compare the dimension of the option picked to the dimension of the option picked on the item with the same id as controlOf (option order is identical between the two, so comparing the chosen letter is equivalent to comparing the chosen dimension). Consistency score = matches / 10.

responsePatternCheck.description: Share of each letter (A/B/C/D) chosen among items 1-100 (control items excluded). With 4 balanced options, chance level is 25% per letter. Flag if any single letter's share is outside 0.10-0.40 (position bias / careless responding).

report.description: Narrative report generator: for each dimension, pick the band ('Low' if dimensionScore < 0.15, 'Mid' if <= 0.35, else 'High' — thresholds centred on the 25% chance level of a 4-option single pick, not 50%) and use report[code].bands[band] as the paragraph, plus the static strengths/suitableWork/tips lines. For the overall summary: if (max dimension score - min dimension score) < 0.15, use a 'balanced profile' message; otherwise name the dimension with the max score as dominant and the one with the min score as weakest.

bands.Low: The authority relationship isn't the theme that stands out most in your answers: you identify less often with statements about challenging or speaking up to a superior. This may reflect a natural tendency to trust the chain of command rather than question it by default. Worth watching in CRM training: make sure this reserve doesn't turn into hesitation to speak up at the right moment.
bands.Mid: You sit in a middle zone on the authority relationship: you're able to speak up to a superior when the situation clearly calls for it, without making it a systematic reflex. This is a generally well-suited stance for the flight deck, where assertiveness should stay proportionate to context.
bands.High: The authority relationship clearly stands out in your answers: you often identify with statements that value questioning, raising a concern, or contradicting a superior when justified. This is an asset for flight safety, provided this assertiveness is always expressed with the tact and respect expected within a crew.

AUTH.strengths: Ability to constructively speak up to the hierarchy when safety or work quality requires it.
AUTH.suitableWork: Roles that require challenging established decisions (flight safety, instruction, quality control).
AUTH.tips: Keep expressing disagreement with tact: substance matters as much as delivery in a cockpit.

bands.Low: Safety values come through less often than other themes in your choices. This doesn't mean a lack of concern for safety, just that this theme isn't what dominates your self-image compared to the nine other dimensions tested. A point to work on: make sure safety stays a priority automatically, without needing to think about it explicitly.
bands.Mid: Safety values hold a consistent place in your profile, neither dominant nor understated. You seem able to balance efficiency and caution depending on context, which fits a well-balanced stance for a future aviation professional.
bands.High: Safety values stand out strongly in your answers: you very often identify with statements placing safety above performance or schedule. This is a central strength for the pilot profession, provided you keep the ability to stay efficient day-to-day without this caution becoming excessive rigidity.

SEC.strengths: Natural priority given to safety, even under time or performance pressure.
SEC.suitableWork: Any operational role where the smallest procedural shortcut has direct safety consequences.
SEC.tips: Keep this vigilance without letting it slow down efficiency on tasks with no safety stakes.

bands.Low: Resilience under stress isn't the most prominent trait in your profile: statements about staying calm under pressure or bouncing back quickly after an incident come through less often in your choices. Worth monitoring in training, especially during high-workload simulator sessions.
bands.Mid: Your stress resilience sits in a middle zone: you seem able to cope with pressure without it being systematically the trait that defines you most. This is consistent with a profile that manages stress case by case rather than through an unshakeable temperament.
bands.High: Resilience clearly stands out in your profile: you often identify with statements about staying calm under pressure, bouncing back quickly after an incident, and not being thrown off by failure. This is a valuable asset in a profession where stress management directly affects the safety of decisions.

RESIL.strengths: Emotional stability and the ability to stay operational after a surprise or a mistake.
RESIL.suitableWork: Roles with high mental workload or repeated exposure to emergency situations.
RESIL.tips: Train regularly on high-workload simulator sessions to reinforce this strength.

bands.Low: Long-term professional motivation comes through less than other themes in your answers. This may simply reflect a profile where other dimensions (technical, relational) are more central to your self-image, without calling your actual commitment into question. Worth watching over time: the risk of burnout from routine.
bands.Mid: Your professional motivation sits in a middle zone: you seem engaged without this being the most prominent trait in your profile. This is a common and healthy stance that leaves room for other personal drivers.
